articles.title: US Vaccine Skepticism Spreads to Australia
articles.content: Experts say the effects of Donald Trump’s rhetoric are already being seen in Australia, with more and more parents having concerns about vaccination. Photograph: Phanie/Sipa Press/Alamy View image in fullscreen Experts say the effects of Donald Trump’s rhetoric are already being seen in Australia, with more and more parents having concerns about vaccination. Photograph: Phanie/Sipa Press/Alamy Australian health experts fear US vaccine scepticism is catching on as ‘anything Trump says filters through’ Australia records 3% fall in one-year-olds fully immunised against hepatitis B as downward trend continues, expert says Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian medical experts have warned a shift in child vaccination advice in the US is not grounded in science and could undo decades of public health advances. The US president, Donald Trump, signed an unprecedented executive order calling for American children to be vaccinated against fewer diseases, suggesting a link to autism despite no evidence. The official number of recommended immunisations for children would drop to 11, compared with 18 at the end of 2024. Six of those shots would be recommended for all children in the US, while the five others would only be recommended for high-risk children, including hepatitis B. Australia currently recommends 15 childhood vaccinations, all of which health experts say are key to protecting children’s health. Prof Julie Leask, a social scientist at the University of Sydney and an expert on social behaviours surrounding vaccination, said Trump’s decision, and his broader embrace of the US health secretary and vaccine opponent, Robert F Kennedy Jr, are threats to vaccine uptake in Australia. “Anything Trump says filters through to Australia,” Leask said. “Australian parents and caregivers hear it, and it does affect a minority of people and makes them wonder about vaccines and their safety.” Leask, a trained midwife, has studied vaccination rates for decades. She said health professionals are already seeing the impacts of Trump’s rhetoric in Australia, with nurses saying they hear from more and more parents who have concerns about vaccination. “Some of my colleagues are worried that we’re kind of going back to the future,” she said. A national survey of Australian parents released in February showed parents were less accepting of routine childhood vaccinations than they were in the previous year. Figures from the Australian immunisation register show full childhood vaccination rates peaking between 2020 and 2021. The coverage rate for all children at five years old is now 92.6%, short of the 95% target. Lucy Clynes, the chief executive of Hepatitis Australia, is extremely concerned about the effect Trump’s policies have had on Australian vaccine confidence. The group analysed search term trends over the past 12 months and found whenever the US government makes comments undercutting the effectiveness or safety of vaccines, Australians head online in greater numbers looking to bolster those claims. “There has been a 3% drop in the number of one-year-olds who are fully immunised for hepatitis B in Australia, a downward trend since about 2020,” Clynes said. “People here see something that the US government has said and they start searching on Google or Instagram, and the results that they get are often wrong. They’re very scary. “When people start doing their own research on vaccines, it means they haven’t immediately trusted what their healthcare provider has told them … And that worries us.” skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion Trump signs executive order with plan to reduce number of recommended childhood vaccines Read more Hepatitis B is a viral infection of the liver and the most common blood-borne virus in Australia. Most people who get infected will develop chronic, lifelong infection that can, after many years, damage the liver and cause diseases including liver cancer and cirrhosis. There is no cure, and more than 230,000 Australians live with chronic hepatitis B infection. Vaccination offers a high degree of protection. Infants in Australia are recommended to get a course of four vaccines to prevent hepatitis B, including one at birth, which can prevent infection even if a mother is positive herself. Prof Ben Cowie, director of the WHO Collaborating Centre for Viral Hepatitis, says vaccination efforts for hepatitis B have been an incredible boon for public health in Australia, saving thousands of lives. “We know that [vaccination programs are] having a profound impact, particularly in high prevalence countries, many of which are in our region,” Cowie said. But vaccine hesitancy is rising and there is a downward trend in childhood vaccination rates, despite an inoculation like the hepatitis B jab being given to billions of people and shown to be incredibly safe and effective. “We can’t ignore that,” Cowie said. The Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases issued a statement for parents stressing the vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) is safe and there is no scientific rationale to change the way that kids in Australia and New Zealand should receive it. Trump’s executive order means the single-injection shot will be split into three appointments. The body attached 10 published studies to the release, showing the MMR vaccine is scientifically safe and effective as given. “ASID encourages parents who have questions about vaccination to speak with their GP, paediatrician, immunisation nurse or other trusted healthcare professional,” the group said. “The science has not changed: MMR vaccination is a safe and effective way to protect children from measles, mumps and rubella.” Explore more on these topics Health Donald Trump Vaccines and immunisation news Share Reuse this content

articles.content: Espanjan ja Marokon viranomaiset valmistautuivat mahdolliseen uuteen rajanylitysten aaltoon Marokosta Ceutan kaupunkiin. Marokon turvallisuusjoukot ilmoittivat lauantaina pysäyttäneensä lähes 300 siirtolaista, enimmäkseen Saharan eteläpuolisesta Afrikasta, jotka yrittivät ylittää maan ja Ceutan välisen rajan, kertoo espanjalainen Cadena Ser . Espanjan uutistoimisto EFE:n mukaan Marokon viranomaiset pidättivät myös 61 muuta ihmistä, joita epäillään ”laittomaan maahanmuuttoon yllyttämisestä”. Marokon turvallisuusjoukot ja rajanylitystä yrittäneet ihmisjoukot ottivat yhteen vuoristoisella alueella noin kolmen kilometrin päässä Ceutan rajalta. Turvallisuusjoukot käyttivät kyynelkaasua ihmisjoukkojen hajottamiseksi. Espanjalaislehti El Mundo uutisoi, että tilanne Ceutan Tarajalin rajanylityspaikalla oli lauantaiaamuna varsin rauhallinen. Rajanylityspaikan läheisyyteen ei lehden mukaan ollut kokoontunut lainkaan ihmisjoukkoja. Sekä Espanja että Marokko vahvistivat viikonlopun kynnyksellä rajavalvontaansa maiden välisellä rajalla. Vaikka Marokon viranomaiset osallistuivat turvatoimien tiukentamiseen Marokon puolella rajaa, ovat Espanjan ja Marokon välit yhä jännittyneet. Espanjalaislehti El Paísin mukaan Marokon sisäministeriön edustaja määräsi lauantaina EFE:n ja Espanjan yleisradioyhtiö RTVE:n toimittajat poistumaan Fnideqistä, jossa nämä raportoivat siirtolaistilanteesta Ceutan läheisyydessä. Fnideq sijaitsee aivan Espanjan ja Marokon välisen rajan tuntumassa. Syy espanjalaistoimittajien karkottamispäätökselle ei toistaiseksi ole tiedossa. El País kertoo EFE:n ottaneen yhteyttä Marokon sisäministeriöön selvittääkseen asiaa. Kymmenettuhannet ihmiset tulivat heinä-elokuun vaihteessa Marokosta rajan yli Espanjalle kuuluvaan Ceutaan. articles.title: Lego's Supersized Hubble Deserves More Shine
articles.content: Excellent internal detail cannot entirely disguise some penny-pinching choices Richard Speed Richard Speed MICROSOFT ECOSYSTEM REPORTER Published sat 15 Aug 2026 // 09:32 UTC Lego has released its largest Hubble Space Telescope yet – a model built at approximately minifig scale that dwarfs the observatory included with its Space Shuttle Discovery set. The first thing to say about this set is that there is an awful lot of grey. This is perhaps the greatest weakness of an otherwise excellent set and feels a little penny-pinching on the part of the Danish brick botherer. Lego has produced several versions of Hubble over the years. There is a version to fit in the payload bay of its large Space Shuttle Discovery set , and a much smaller incarnation on a plinth in the Women of NASA set . Both are retired, so scratching that Hubble itch with a current official set means dropping £119.99 on the Icons Hubble Space Telescope. It's a large set. According to Lego, the 1,252-piece set measures 32 cm tall, 38 cm long (with the aperture door open), and 38 cm wide. An astronaut minifigure is included to indicate the model's approximate scale – a shame there's just one, since the servicing missions had a pair of spacewalkers – along with a power tool. There is also a stand featuring some of Hubble's iconic imagery and a plaque with more information, including the dates of the Space Shuttle servicing missions. Lego has not included replacement instruments to recreate the various servicing activities. Inside are Lego representations of Hubble's instruments and systems, including its gyroscopes, primary mirror, and secondary mirror. Outside are posable solar arrays and antennas, along with an aperture door that opens. Some parts are a little fiddly, and the set is aimed at ages 18+. That seems a little on the high side, but this isn't something you'd want a young child trying to build. The level of detail is impressive, considering the nature of Lego components, but it is difficult to avoid all that grey plastic. The Hubble Space Telescope included with the Space Shuttle Discovery Icons set uses silver bricks, which makes the choice of grey plastic feel cheap in comparison. Lego's Space Shuttle Discovery: No trouble with Hubble, but the stickers will drive a grown man to insanity Is that... is that a piece of Unikitty? Remembering Skylab via the medium of Lego Building the Apollo Soyuz Test Project out of Lego Hubble in a death spiral that could end as early as 2028 without a reboost And then there are the stickers. Thankfully, there aren't too many, but printed parts are readily available, and Lego uses its own, so why make builders fiddle with sticker alignment? And then there are the solar arrays, which are single-sided and feel a little cheap compared with the arrays on some of the MOCs The Register has built over the years .  Still, these are minor niggles in what is otherwise a fun build lasting 6-12 hours. The set is an excellent addition to the Icons range, but such is the affection for Hubble that details matter. The set also acknowledges Hubble's 35th anniversary, celebrated in April 2025, with a "35" decal on the back of the astronaut minifigure. The real thing continues to orbit, although its days are likely numbered .  The Lego version is likely to endure until a careless elbow knocks it off the shelf, or a creative builder decides to repurpose its components for an orbital animal amusement park. Which, after all, is the whole point. ® lego hubble space telescope offbeat nasa
